PostgreSQL implements the standard B-tree index structure, a multi-way balanced tree.
B-tree indexes support any data type with a well-defined linear sort order.
A B-tree index entry cannot exceed approximately one-third of a page after applicable TOAST compression.
PostgreSQL uses B-tree operator classes and operator families to represent sorting semantics throughout the system.
A B-tree operator class must provide five comparison operators.
The inequality operator is excluded from B-tree operator classes because inequality conditions are almost never useful for index searches.
The PostgreSQL planner associates inequality with a B-tree operator class through the equality operator's negator link rather than pg_amop.
Operator classes with near-identical sorting semantics can share an operator family, allowing planner deductions about cross-type comparisons.
Each operator class should contain its input type's single-type operators and support functions; cross-type operators and support functions belong loosely to the family.
A complete set of cross-type operators is recommended so the planner can represent comparison conditions deduced through transitivity.
B-tree equality must form an equivalence relation over non-null values, satisfying reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity.
B-tree ordering must be a strong total ordering over non-null values, satisfying irreflexivity, transitivity, and trichotomy.
The remaining three B-tree comparison operators must behave consistently with equality and ordering.
B-tree operator-family laws must hold across all combinations of supported data types; planner optimizations rely on consistency across three or more types.
Current numeric-to-float8 comparison semantics prevent numeric and float8 from sharing a B-tree operator family because limited float8 precision breaks equality transitivity.
Implicit casts and binary-coercion casts between types in a B-tree operator family must preserve the associated sort order.
B-tree defines one required support function and four optional support functions.
Every supported comparison type pair requires a comparison function registered in pg_amproc as support function 1 with matching left and right types.
B-tree comparison functions accept two non-null values and return an int32 indicating less-than, equality, or greater-than; null results are prohibited.
Comparison functions for collatable types receive the appropriate collation OID through the standard PG_GET_COLLATION() mechanism.
Optional sort support functions use support function number 2 and enable more efficient sorting comparisons; src/include/utils/sortsupport.h defines the APIs.
Optional in_range functions use support function number 3 and support RANGE window-frame bounds rather than B-tree index operations.
The in_range support function specifies offset addition or subtraction compatible with an operator family's ordering.
The in_range value and base arguments must share a family-supported type; the offset can have another type, including a type unsupported by the family.
The built-in time_ops operator family provides an in_range function with an interval offset.
The PostgreSQL source file src/backend/access/nbtree/README provides a detailed, internals-focused description of B-tree implementation.
PostgreSQL B-tree indexes have multiple levels, each usable as a doubly linked list of pages.
A B-tree index stores one metapage at a fixed position at the start of its first segment file.
All non-metapage B-tree pages are leaf or internal pages; leaf pages occupy the lowest level and typically exceed 99% of all pages.
Leaf-page tuples point to table rows; internal-page tuples point to the next lower tree level; both page types use PostgreSQL's standard page format.
An incoming tuple that cannot fit on a leaf page triggers a split that moves some existing items to a new leaf page.
Page splits require new parent downlinks and can cascade upward; splitting the root creates a new root and adds a tree level.
B-tree indexes treat each physical table-row version as an independent object requiring an index entry, without directly recognizing MVCC logical-row relationships.
Accumulated version-churn tuples can harm query latency and throughput, particularly in UPDATE-heavy workloads where most updates cannot use HOT optimization.
Changing even one indexed column during UPDATE requires successor tuples in every table index, including indexes whose indexed values remain unchanged.
Successor index tuples point to the latest table-row version and generally coexist briefly with the original index tuples.
Bottom-up deletion incrementally removes version-churn tuples when a version-churn page split is anticipated in an index not logically modified by UPDATE.
Bottom-up deletion targets suspected garbage in one leaf page using qualitative distinctions between logical rows and physical versions.
Bottom-up deletion usually avoids page splits; unsuccessful deletion heuristics can leave a page split or deduplication pass necessary to accommodate an incoming tuple.
The worst-case number of versions an index scan traverses for one logical row significantly affects system responsiveness and throughput.
Autovacuum performs top-down index cleanup when quantitative table-level thresholds are exceeded.
Simple deletion removes tuples already marked LP_DEAD by recent index scans and runs when a page split is anticipated; PostgreSQL before 14 supported only simple deletion.
For suitable workloads, bottom-up deletion performs most garbage cleanup, keeps version counts low, and can prevent index growth despite constant version churn.
An exhaustive VACUUM sweep, typically performed by autovacuum, remains necessary because bottom-up deletion provides no strong guarantee about the oldest garbage tuple's age.
A shared conservative cutoff prevents indexes retaining older dead tuples, enabling safe table-TID recycling and reuse by distinct logical rows over time.
